items.value: The gains of economic reform reach agriculture more slowly than they reach the other sectors
items.reasoning: The passage's whole content is a contrast: agriculture peaked at a 3.5% decadal CAGR and then stagnated, while non-agricultural growth 'consistently increased from the 1980s to 2000s'. The corollary that stays inside that contrast is that whatever lifted the non-farm economy over those decades percolated to agriculture far more slowly. B, C and D each import something the passage never mentions - the green revolution, a comparison with other countries, and rural-to-urban migration - so none of them can be a corollary of this text.

The passage is purely descriptive: it reports growth rates and their divergence and offers no diagnosis and no remedy. Assumption I (commercial crops and corporate farming) and Assumption II (free crop insurance plus heavy subsidy on seeds, fertilizers, electricity and machinery 'at par with developed countries') are both policy prescriptions the text neither states nor takes for granted, and II is additionally an extreme, absolute claim of the kind the passage nowhere supports. Neither survives, so D.

items.value: Handloom must be freed from the narrow 'preserving cultural heritage' narrative
items.reasoning: The author's argument runs: handloom is equated with tradition, that equation is the basis of State support, but the idea of tradition as a single linear entity is contested because dominant narratives stifled other identities - so 'when we promote handloom as a traditional industry, it is not surprising that large sections choose to ignore it.' The logical message is therefore to stop confining handloom to the heritage narrative, which is A. B restates the very position the author is criticising; C (modernise into an organised industry) and D (machine-made designer products) are prescriptions found nowhere in the text, and D would contradict handloom itself.

Assumption I is invalid because the author questions the *narrative* used to justify State support, not State involvement itself - the passage calls that basis 'legitimate' and never argues for withdrawal, let alone 'in any manner'. Assumption II is invalid because the passage attributes the indifference of large sections to the traditional-industry framing and to contested identity, not to the products having lost appeal. Neither is presupposed, so D.

9 is redundant here, since every multiple of 9 is already a multiple of 3, so the condition reduces to 'not divisible by 2, 3, 5 or 7'. By inclusion-exclusion the count of numbers in 1-100 divisible by at least one of them is (50+33+20+14) - (16+10+7+6+4+2) + (3+2+1+0) = 78, leaving 100 - 78 = 22. The surviving numbers are 1 together with the 21 primes from 11 to 97 (no composite below 100 avoids all four, since the smallest such composite is 11 x 11 = 121), which confirms 22.

items.value: None of the above - the ratio is -5, which is not printed
items.reasoning: The maximum of (x + y) is 8 + 7 = 15. The minimum of (x - y) takes the smallest x with the largest y, that is 4 - 7 = -3, not 2. The required ratio is therefore 15 / (-3) = -5, which appears in none of the first three options, so D. Option B (15/2) is the trap for taking the minimum of x minus the minimum of y.

items.value: 5 possible values of k, namely 2, 3, 7, 13 and 19
items.reasoning: If p is odd then p squared is odd, so p squared + k can only be an odd prime when k is even, forcing k = 2; that works for p = 3 (9 + 2 = 11) but not p = 5 (27 is composite), and p = 7 already exceeds 30. If p = 2 then 4 + k must be an odd prime under 30, which holds for k = 3 (7), 7 (11), 13 (17) and 19 (23), while k = 5, 11, 17 and 23 give the composites 9, 15, 21 and 27. The distinct values of k are therefore {2, 3, 7, 13, 19}, so 5.

1001 = 7 x 11 x 13, so each of the three numbers is a product of some subset of {7, 11, 13}; LCM 1001 means every prime appears in at least one number and HCF 1 means every prime is missing from at least one. Each prime independently admits 2 cubed - 2 = 6 allowed patterns across the three slots, giving 216 ordered triples, which reduces to 32 sets of three distinct numbers (for example {1, 7, 143}, {7, 11, 13}, {11, 91, 143}). Every reasonable reading - ordered, unordered, or requiring distinct entries - is far above 8, so D.

Writing the subtraction out, (100P + 10Q + R) - (10P + S) = 110P + T reduces with Q = 3 to R - S = 20P + T - 30. Since R - S must lie between -8 and 8, P = 2 is impossible (it forces R - S at least 11), so P = 1 and R - S = T - 10 with T in {2, 4, 5} (T is under 6 and cannot equal P = 1 or Q = 3). This yields exactly 132 - 18 = 114, 132 - 17 = 115 and 134 - 19 = 115, giving the three pairs (2, 8), (2, 7) and (4, 9); T = 2 fails because it would need R = 1 = P.

The 18-character string is the block ABBCCC repeated three times: ABBCCC ABBCCC ABBCCC. Every printed letter matches this block exactly - positions 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, 10, 11, 12, 14, 15, 16 and 18 all agree - so the five gaps at positions 3, 6, 8, 13 and 17 must be B, C, B, A and C. Only option C gives that sequence.

items.value: The classroom must be reimagined and teaching re-invented
items.reasoning: The passage contrasts our exam-driven teaching with what society and the future of work now demand - critical thinking, learning by doing, multi-disciplinary questioning, evidence and articulation - and closes with the explicit sentence 'Teaching has to be re-invented.' D captures that. A (resources) is never mentioned; B overstates a quoted phrase about not being a servant of government policy into a demand for autonomy from government; and C is too extreme, since the author wants the classroom transformed, not abolished.

The passage's entire argument - that 'the new demands of society and the future of work' require a different kind of learning and that teaching must therefore be re-invented - presupposes that higher education has to keep aligning itself with what is changing around it, which is Assumption I. Assumption II is invalid because funding is never mentioned anywhere in the text. The one judgement call is I's sweeping phrase 'all spheres of society', but that is a fair reading of a passage that itself invokes multiple disciplinary perspectives and the future of work.

items.value: Converting plant food into animal food is highly inefficient compared with eating plants directly
items.reasoning: The passage's core evidence is the conversion loss: grains and legumes that could feed people directly are fed to poultry and livestock, and we recover only 16% of the calories from chickens and just five to seven per cent from large animals. B states exactly that. A and C are policy prescriptions (promote cereals, replace animal protein) the author never makes, and D asserts that inequality is 'inevitable', which the passage does not claim.

Assumption II follows directly from the passage: wealthier societies eat more animal products, so their grain is routed indirectly through livestock, and the stated recovery rates of 16% and five to seven per cent are precisely a large calorie loss. Assumption I is invalid because the passage says nothing about food manufacturing or processing industries, or about what they should align their objectives to. The judgement call is that II reads as an inference drawn from the text rather than a hidden premise, but it is plainly supported while I is not, so B.

Since 35 = 5 x 7, count each prime separately. Powers of 7: 7 gives 1, 343 gives 3, 385 gives 1, 2401 gives 4 and 77777 = 7 x 41 x 271 gives 1, totalling 10. Powers of 5: only 385 (one 5) and 1000 (three 5s), totalling 4. The limiting prime is 5, so the largest n is min(10, 4) = 4; the product is divisible by 35 to the fourth power but not the fifth.

Read the sequence as successive multipliers rather than differences: 12 to 18 is x1.5, 18 to 36 is x2 and 36 to 90 is x2.5, so the multipliers rise by 0.5 each step. Extending backwards, the earlier multipliers must be x1 and x0.5, giving 24 x 0.5 = 12 and then 12 x 1 = 12. The full sequence 24, 12, 12, 18, 36, 90 has multipliers 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5 throughout, so X = 12.

items.value: 14 crossings, the last of them falling exactly at 7:00 a.m.
items.reasoning: Walking in opposite directions their relative speed is 5 + 3 = 8 rounds per hour, so they meet every 60/8 = 7.5 minutes, at 5:07:30, 5:15, 5:22:30 and so on. Over the two hours from 5:00 to 7:00 there are 16 meetings, of which 2 occur before 5:20, leaving 14 - but the sixteenth falls exactly at 7:00 a.m. This item is ambiguous as printed: counting that boundary meeting gives 14, while reading 'between 5:20 a.m. and 7:00 a.m.' as strictly excluding 7:00 gives 13, and both numbers are offered as options. I take the inclusive reading, but 13 is equally defensible and the question should be flagged.

Substituting the code and applying BODMAS, option B reads 60 - 15 x 3 + 20 / 4 = 60 - 45 + 5 = 20, which matches. The others fail: A gives 60 / 15 + 3 x 20 - 4 = 60, C gives 60 - 15 x 3 / 20 + 4 = 61.75, and D gives 60 / 15 + 3 - 20 x 4 = -73.

Let the tram's speed be v km/hr. Passing a person means covering the tram's own length at the relative speed, so the length equals 8 x (v - 3) x 5/18 and also 9 x (v - 4) x 5/18. Equating gives 8v - 24 = 9v - 36, so v = 12 km/hr, and the length is 8 x 9 x 5/18 = 20 m (checked against the second person: 9 x 8 x 5/18 = 20 m).

The palindrome 12345678987654321 is the square of the repunit 111111111, which has nine 1s - this is the familiar pattern where 11 squared is 121, 111 squared is 12321, and so on up to nine digits. Verified directly: 111111111 x 111111111 = 12345678987654321 exactly, so N has 9 digits.
